newsitem.title: GERMANY: INSTANT VIEW - German December manufacturing orders.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - German December manufacturing orders.

text.p: Following are reactions to German manufacturing orders for December showing a 1.4 percent fall from November's revised 0.5 percent drop. Economists had forecast a 3.3 percent rise.

STEFAN BERGHEIM, economist at Kleinwort Benson in Frankfurt. "The numbers were much weaker than expected and the string of data we have had recently, including the ifo confidence report and output, show a very contradictory picture. We need to look at all the numbers, and in the end they would likely give a neutral reading for the economy. The Bundesbank will not act on these numbers."

STEFAN BERGHEIM added "The best thing for the Bundesbank to do now is nothing after M3 money supply and inflation were all higher recently. The bond market on the other hand liked the numbers, but the price gains may also be motivated by the market's desire to find numbers that give reasons for prices to climb further."

KLAUS HOLSCHUH, head of bonds research at Commerzbank in Frankfurt. "The numbers were much worse than we forecast, but it is important to realise special factors impacted the data this year and that these numbers are often sharply revised in later months."

KLAUS HOLSCHUH added, "When the numbers are viewed alongside Tuesday's stronger than expected output numbers, then the indication is neutral for the economy. Consequently the Bundesbank will not adjust its policy on back of these numbers. These numbers in no way indicate a change in the trend."

ECKHARD SCHULTE, economist at IBJ Bank in Frankfurt. "The numbers, which are much worse than expected, show that the economy is still in a very weak state. What is extremely worrying is the weakness of investments. This indicates that the upswing, which everyone is expecting some time this year, may actually be pushed out further."

"The numbers today indicate that we may be seeing a repeat of last year's scenario and that first quarter gross domestic product in 1997 will show a fall not rise." --Svea Herbst-Bayliss, Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525
